slides.speaker_notes: Welcome to this graduate lecture on backpropagation. By the end, you will understand backprop not as a mysterious learning algorithm, but as an efficient gradient computer built on the chain rule and dynamic programming. We will start by clarifying a common misconception — that backprop defines the weight update — and then build the machinery layer by layer. The lecture culminates in two real-world case studies: one from medical image segmentation, and one from financial risk systems. Let's begin.

slides.title: Backprop Is the Gradient Computer, Not the Learning Rule
bullets: Backpropagation computes all partial derivatives of a scalar cost in one backward pass
It reuses intermediate results so total computation scales like two forward passes
Finite differences would require over a million forward passes for a million-parameter network
The optimizer — SGD, Adam, RMSProp — decides how to use the gradient vector
Separating gradient computation from optimization is essential for debugging training failures
slides.speaker_notes: Let's start with the most important clarification. Backpropagation is not a learning algorithm. It does not define how to update weights. It is purely a gradient computer: it takes a scalar cost J and efficiently produces the gradient vector with respect to every parameter. The optimizer then decides what to do with that vector — subtract a fraction, add momentum, adaptively scale it. If you confuse these two, you cannot debug whether a training failure comes from a bug in your gradient code or a poor choice of learning rate. We keep them separate throughout this lecture.

slides.title: Four Prerequisites You Must Have Before We Start
bullets: Apply the scalar chain rule dz/dx = (dz/dy)*(dy/dx) to nested functions
Read a directed acyclic graph where nodes are operations and edges carry data
Multiply matrices and vectors, and know that ∂(Wx)/∂x = W
Define a feedforward layer: affine transform z = Wa + b followed by element-wise nonlinearity
If any of these four feels shaky, pause and review them now before proceeding
slides.speaker_notes: We are going to build every new idea on top of these four foundations. If you are comfortable applying the chain rule to nested scalar functions, reading a DAG, multiplying matrices, and defining a feedforward layer, you are ready. If not, this is the moment to review. The entire backpropagation derivation that follows is just these four ideas composed systematically. There is no additional magic.

slides.title: The Computation Graph Is a City Map for Gradient Flow
bullets: Each intersection in the graph is an operation: addition, multiplication, ReLU
The forward pass drives from input to cost, recording every intermediate activation
The backward pass sends the gradient of the cost back to every parameter
Each intersection knows only its local derivative — how output changes when input changes
Backprop multiplies local derivatives along every path and sums paths that meet at a node
slides.speaker_notes: Imagine a city where each intersection is an operation. The forward pass drives from the input to the cost, recording the route. The backward pass wants to send a message — the gradient of the cost — back to every parameter. Each intersection knows only its local derivative. Backpropagation is the postal service that delivers the gradient by multiplying local derivatives along every path, then summing paths that meet. This is exactly the chain rule, organized so we never recompute a path we already walked.

slides.title: The Chain Rule on a Graph: Sum Over Children
slides.equation_tex: \frac{\partial z}{\partial u} = \sum_{\text{children } v \text{ of } u} \frac{\partial z}{\partial v} \cdot \frac{\partial v}{\partial u}
slides.equation_caption: The gradient at node u is the sum of gradient signals from all its downstream children, each multiplied by the local derivative.
bullets: The sum appears because a node can feed into multiple downstream operations
Reverse topological order guarantees children are processed before parents
Without reverse order, shared sub-expressions would be recomputed exponentially many times
This dynamic programming insight is what makes backpropagation efficient
slides.speaker_notes: Here is the central equation. For any intermediate node u in the graph, the gradient of the scalar cost z with respect to u is the sum over all children v of u of the gradient at v multiplied by the local derivative ∂v/∂u. Why a sum? Because if u feeds into two different operations — say a weight used in both layer 1 and a skip connection — both paths carry gradient information back to u. The chain rule adds them. Reverse topological order guarantees we process children before parents, avoiding exponential recomputation of shared sub-expressions.

slides.title: Backpropagation as Circuit Sensitivity Analysis
slides.equation_caption: The gradient through an activation function is an element-wise product with the derivative of f evaluated at the pre-activation.
bullets: This is a vector-Jacobian product: the Jacobian of f is a diagonal matrix diag(f'(z))
For ReLU, f'(z) = 1[z > 0] — gradient flows only through active units
For sigmoid, f'(z) = σ(z)(1-σ(z)) = a_out ⊙ (1 - a_out)
Dead ReLU units receive zero gradient and stop learning permanently
slides.speaker_notes: This equation is the hidden gradient propagation step. Once we have the gradient with respect to the activation output, we push it backward through the nonlinearity. The operation is an element-wise product with the derivative of the activation function evaluated at the pre-activation values. This is a vector-Jacobian product in disguise: the Jacobian of an element-wise function is a diagonal matrix, and multiplying a row vector by a diagonal matrix is exactly the Hadamard product. For ReLU, this means gradient flows only through units with positive pre-activation — dead units get zero gradient and stop learning. This is the dying ReLU problem.

slides.title: Weight Gradient as an Outer Product
slides.equation_caption: The gradient for a weight matrix is the outer product of the pre-activation gradient (transposed) and the input activation.
bullets: A weight W_{ij} receives gradient proportional to the signal at output i and the activation of input j
If either factor is zero, the weight gets no gradient — it was irrelevant or its input was silent
This is a rank-1 matrix per sample; the batch gradient sums many such outer products
The bias gradient is simply the sum of the incoming gradient vector: ∂J/∂b = sum(∂J/∂z)
slides.speaker_notes: Now we reach the weight update. The gradient for a weight matrix W is the outer product of the gradient with respect to the pre-activation outputs and the input activations. Concretely, each element W_{ij} receives a contribution proportional to how much output i needs to change and how strongly input j was active. If either is zero, that connection gets no update. This is a rank-1 matrix per training example; when we process a batch, we sum many such outer products. The bias gradient is simpler — just the sum of the incoming gradient vector. This is why bias terms learn even when some inputs are zero.

slides.title: The Three-Step Backward Pass for a Single Layer
bullets: Step 1: Receive gradient of the loss with respect to the layer's output activations
Step 2: Push through the activation function using element-wise product with f'(z)
Step 3: Compute weight gradient as outer product of output gradient and input activation
Step 4: Propagate gradient to the previous layer by multiplying with W^T
This three-step pattern repeats identically for every layer in the network
slides.speaker_notes: Let's unify the three equations we just derived into a single recipe. For any layer, the backward pass has three steps. First, receive the gradient with respect to the output activations from the layer above. Second, push it through the activation function by element-wise multiplying with the derivative. Third, compute the weight gradient as the outer product of the resulting vector and the input activation. Fourth — and this is the propagation step — multiply by the transpose of the weight matrix to send the gradient to the previous layer. This four-step pattern is the entire backpropagation algorithm. Every layer repeats it identically.

slides.title: Why Backprop Is Efficient: Dynamic Programming
bullets: Each intermediate gradient is computed once and reused by all upstream paths
Without this caching, gradient computation would be exponential in network depth
Reverse-mode automatic differentiation is the general name for this technique
Frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow build the graph and run this automatically
The forward pass cost is roughly 1x; the backward pass adds about 1.5x–2x
slides.speaker_notes: The efficiency of backprop comes from dynamic programming. Each intermediate gradient — say the gradient at a hidden layer — is computed once and then reused by all paths that flow through it. If we did naive forward-mode differentiation, we would have to recompute the same sub-expressions for every parameter, leading to exponential cost. Reverse-mode automatic differentiation — the general name for backprop — avoids this by caching. In practice, the backward pass costs about 1.5 to 2 times the forward pass. This is why we can train models with hundreds of millions of parameters on commodity hardware.

slides.title: Common Failure Modes: Vanishing and Exploding Gradients
bullets: Vanishing gradients: products of many small derivatives shrink exponentially in depth
Exploding gradients: products of many large derivatives grow exponentially and destabilize training
Sigmoid and tanh saturate at ±1 with near-zero derivatives, causing vanishing
ReLU mitigates vanishing by passing gradient 1 for positive inputs
Residual connections and batch normalization add bypass paths that preserve gradient magnitude
slides.speaker_notes: The chain rule multiplies many local derivatives. If those derivatives are consistently smaller than 1, the product shrinks exponentially — vanishing gradients. If they are larger than 1, the product explodes. Both are catastrophic. Sigmoid and tanh are particularly prone to vanishing because their derivatives approach zero at saturation. ReLU fixes this for positive inputs by passing gradient 1. But the real solutions for very deep networks are architectural: residual connections add identity bypass paths, and batch normalization keeps activations in a regime with healthy gradient flow.

slides.title: Try It: Two-Layer Network With ReLU
slides.exercise_prompt: Given y = w2 * relu(w1 * x + b1) + b2 and squared loss L = (y - t)^2 with x = 1.0, t = 0.5, w1 = 0.8, w2 = -1.2, b1 = 0.1, b2 = 0.0: (a) compute the forward pass; (b) derive dL/dw1 by hand; (c) report which term vanishes when w1 * x + b1 < 0.
bullets: Hint: ReLU's derivative is the indicator 1[z > 0]
Hint: chain through the output, then the activation, then the linear layer
Discuss why a negative pre-activation kills the gradient signal
slides.speaker_notes: Give students four minutes. The goal is to feel the chain rule unroll layer by layer. They should produce one term per layer, with ReLU contributing an indicator function that switches off when the pre-activation is negative. The vanishing case is the entire point — it explains why dead ReLUs and bad initialization matter in practice.

slides.title: Case Study 1: U-Net for Medical Image Segmentation
bullets: U-Net stacks dozens of convolutional layers with skip connections across depths
The skip connections create multiple gradient paths: one short, one long
The short path preserves high-resolution spatial gradient; the long path captures semantic context
Without skip connections, the deepest layers receive vanishing gradients and fail to learn
Training uses Dice loss, a soft variant of intersection-over-union, with Adam optimizer
slides.speaker_notes: Let's see backprop in action in a real architecture. U-Net for medical image segmentation has a contracting path and an expanding path, with skip connections that concatenate features from early layers to later layers. These skip connections create multiple gradient paths: a short, direct path that preserves high-resolution spatial information, and a long path through the bottleneck that captures semantic context. Without skip connections, the deepest layers would receive vanishing gradients and fail to learn. The Dice loss — a soft approximation of intersection-over-union — is differentiated by backprop, and Adam adaptively scales the resulting gradients.

slides.title: Case Study 2: Gradient-Based Risk Attribution in Finance
bullets: A pricing model maps market factors (rates, volatilities) to a portfolio value
Backprop computes the sensitivity of portfolio value to every input factor simultaneously
This is a vector-Jacobian product: one backward pass yields all partial derivatives
Finite differences would require repricing the entire portfolio for each factor perturbation
Regulators use these gradients for stress testing and capital allocation under Basel III
slides.speaker_notes: Backprop is not just for neural networks. In quantitative finance, a pricing model maps thousands of market factors — interest rates, volatilities, credit spreads — to a single portfolio value. The risk team needs the sensitivity of that value to every factor. This is exactly a vector-Jacobian product: one backward pass through the pricing model yields all partial derivatives. Finite differences would require repricing the entire portfolio thousands of times — computationally infeasible. Regulators under Basel III use these gradients for stress testing and capital allocation. The same algorithmic principle that trains neural networks powers modern risk management.

slides.title: What To Remember About Backpropagation
bullets: Backprop is the chain rule applied to a computational graph, nothing more
The forward pass caches activations; the backward pass reuses them
Every parameter receives exactly one gradient per training step
Vanishing gradients motivate ReLU, batch norm, and residual connections
Modern frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow automate this with autograd
slides.speaker_notes: Close by tying the math back to engineering decisions students will actually make: activation choice, weight initialization, network depth, optimizer. The chain rule is the invariant — everything else in modern deep learning is engineering around the failure modes of that single equation. Mention PyTorch autograd as the standard implementation they will use in practice.
